title: Aloud, whispered, silent
hookLine: Krishna calls japa his own offering, and an old law book ranks the silent kind highest
carry: japa is an offering, even in silence
tomorrow: can a name said wrong still work?

cards: Dawn, one house, three people, the same mantra. In the kitchen a grandmother says it out loud while the kettle heats, each syllable clear from the hallway.

On the back step her grandson whispers it, the sound barely past his teeth. Upstairs his mother sits on the edge of the bed with her eyes closed, and nothing moves at all. No lips, no breath out of rhythm.
Walk through that house and you'd only know two of them were doing japa. All three are. An old law book sets those three voices in an order, and the order runs against the ear.

teach.h: IN WHAT FORMS SHOULD I THINK OF YOU?
teach.b: Japa is repetition: a mantra said again and again, often counted on a string of beads. In the Bhagavad Gita, chapter ten, Arjuna asks Krishna a simple question: in what forms should I think of you?
Krishna names the best of many things, and among sacrifices, he says, he is the sacrifice of japa: the offering made of a word. That's the teaching under every mala. Japa isn't a drill.
It's yajna, an offering, the same word used for offerings poured into the sacred fire, made of nothing but a name. The law book called the Manusmriti then ranks the ways of making it.
In its second chapter it says japa is stronger than the prescribed rites.
Japa spoken so that others can't hear it is stronger still. And japa done in the mind alone is the strongest of the three.

Manu calls the quiet form upamshu, sound kept close to the lips, and the silent one manasa, of the mind. Teachers call the spoken form vachika. So the quietest voice in the house is the one the text sets highest.
Some teachers read it this way: when the mantra is loud, the ear holds it for you. Whispered, the lips still help.

teach.h: MOVE BETWEEN THEM AS THE MIND NEEDS.
teach.b: Silent, the mind has nothing to lean on but the mind. For a long sadhana, some teachers suggest moving between the voices rather than forcing silence: back to a whisper when attention scatters, silent when it settles.

teach.h: AN OFFERING MADE OF A WORD.
teach.b: Read that way, the grandmother in the kitchen and the mother upstairs are making the same offering.

how: Hindus who keep japa may say the mantra aloud, in a whisper or silently in the mind, often counting on a mala of beads; some move between these voices within one sitting.

o: a book that lists the meanings of mantras
a mantra kept as a discipline, day after day
a single mantra chanted once at a wedding

games.q: the three voices of japa — tap the pairs.

s: the louder the mantra, the stronger the japa
the Manusmriti ranks it the other way: whispered above spoken, and mental above both.
in the Gita, Krishna names japa among sacrifices
in chapter ten, when Arjuna asks where to see him, he says that among sacrifices he is the sacrifice of japa.
a practice has to stay in one voice the whole time
some teachers suggest moving between voices: back to a whisper when attention scatters, silent when it settles.

games.q: you're keeping a mantra silently, and your mind keeps drifting off mid-count. what do you do?
o: stop for today and try again tomorrow.
go back to a whisper until attention settles.
force the silence and count faster.
games.why: some teachers suggest moving between the voices: let the lips help for a while, then let the sound drop away again.

practice: Take the mantra you've been keeping, or the syllable Om, or a single word from your own tradition, and say it aloud a few times, gently.
Let it become a whisper, lips moving, then close the lips and keep it going inside, with no sound at all. If the mind wanders, go back to the whisper for a while, then let it go silent again.

wordCard.voice: Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, the three voices it can be kept in: spoken, whispered and silent.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: upamshu, the whispered japa, sound kept close to the lips.

carryVoice: Your line: japa is an offering, even in silence. Aloud, whispered or in the mind, Krishna calls it his. Go gently.
